summary:
Orbloom is an offline-first health and well-being app for astronauts on long missions, with a separate dashboard for the flight surgeon on Earth. Astronauts log a private daily check-in (mood, stress, energy, sleep, workload) and record readings like blood pressure and heart rate. Each reading is shown against normal ranges, and a Health assistant explains it in plain words without diagnosing. The app also includes a searchable list of the 95 medicines in NASA’s ISS Medical Kit, a 30-second alertness game, a greenhouse of seven crops astronauts really grew, family messages, and a shared crew garden that nudges crewmates to check in on each other.

It addresses Challenge 4 by making health monitoring work when the doctor is far away and the link to Earth comes and goes. Data is saved and encrypted on the device first and syncs when a connection opens. The flight surgeon sees alerts, readings and an AI summary, but never private check-ins or messages.

It matters because long missions bring isolation, stress and broken sleep, and these problems usually build slowly rather than starting as emergencies. Orbloom looks after astronauts’ health and their connection to each other.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Orbloom is an offline-first health and well-being companion for astronauts on long missions, with a dashboard for the flight surgeon on the ground. On a long mission there is no doctor on board, and the link to Earth comes and goes: toward Mars, one message can take about 20 minutes each way. Most health apps assume you are always online. Orbloom saves everything on the device first, works with no internet, and syncs on its own when a link opens.

For the astronaut:

- Daily check-in: mood, stress, energy, sleep and workload. Private to the device.

- Health: blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature, sleep and blood sugar, each shown against general reference ranges (green, yellow, red) with trend graphs. Red readings create an alert for the flight surgeon.

- Health assistant: an AI that explains readings in plain words. It never diagnoses, and red-flag symptoms skip the AI and go straight to the flight surgeon.

- Medical kit: the 95 medicines of NASA's ISS Medical Kit Checklist, searchable by medicine or symptom with no internet. It is a list, not an AI, so nothing is made up.

- Alertness game: a 30-second reaction test that scores reaction time, accuracy and consistency out of 100 and compares it with the person's usual level.

- Greenhouse: grow one of seven crops NASA astronauts grew on the ISS, with step-by-step care and a daily checklist.

- Family (beta): messages home written offline, sent when a link opens.

- Crew garden: every astronaut has a flower bed in a shared garden. It blooms with check-ins, rest and greenhouse care and wilts when routines slip, so crewmates get a gentle nudge to check in, without seeing any health numbers.

- Get medical help: a help signal to the flight surgeon, sent at once or as soon as the link opens.

For the flight surgeon: health readings, alertness, red-flag alerts and an AI summary for each astronaut. They never see check-in answers, moods, private notes or family messages, and every visit is recorded in an access log.

BENEFITS

- Care that does not wait for a signal.

- Earlier warning: slow changes in readings, sleep or alertness show up before they become emergencies.

- Privacy by design, so crews can answer honestly.

- Support for the whole person: health, alertness, routine, something living to care for, and connection with crew and family.

- Less load on the flight surgeon: red flags and short summaries instead of raw data.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want crews on long missions to get support before, during and between emergencies, not only during them. The same approach can serve analog missions (Mars and Moon simulation habitats), polar stations and other remote crews with poor connectivity. Our next step is testing with flight surgeons and analog-mission crews, and having a flight surgeon review the alert thresholds.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: JavaScript (React), HTML and CSS, SQL (PostgreSQL), TypeScript (server function).

- App: React 19 and Vite, installable on phones and laptops as a web app that works offline. Data is stored and encrypted in the browser's own database (IndexedDB, through Dexie). Charts use Recharts.

- Backend: Supabase (PostgreSQL database with row-level security, sign-in, and an Edge Function that runs the AI so the AI key never reaches the device).

- AI: the open-weight gpt-oss-120b model, run on Groq, for the Health assistant and the flight surgeon's summary. Claude (Anthropic) helped us write the code, documentation and slides.

- Hosting: Vercel and GitHub Pages. Code on GitHub. Testing with Playwright.

- Hardware: none needed. It runs in the browser of any phone or laptop.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- The crew garden turns well-being into something a crew can see and care about together, without exposing anyone's medical data.

- The design treats the broken link as the main problem, not an edge case: help signals and messages wait safely and send themselves.

- The medical kit deliberately uses real NASA data instead of AI, so medicine answers are never invented.

- The greenhouse uses crops astronauts really grew on the ISS, linking daily care to a real piece of space history.

- A calm night-garden look, designed to feel restful in a stressful place.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Communication delays and blackouts: offline-first storage, queued alerts and automatic sync.

- Medical safety: the AI explains but never diagnoses, red flags always go to a human flight surgeon, ranges are labelled as general reference ranges rather than mission limits, and the medicine list is copied from NASA's document.

- Privacy and trust: check-ins, moods and family messages never leave the device; the flight surgeon's access is limited and logged.

- Security: database rules decide who can read what, data is encrypted on the device, and API keys stay on the server.

- Accessibility: a highly readable font (Atkinson Hyperlegible), large touch targets, and a layout that works on phones.

- Cost: built entirely on free tiers, so it is cheap to test with real crews.

- Honesty about limits: family replies are automatic for now (beta), and thresholds still need review by a flight surgeon.
